C001.title: ArmaturaSec d.o.o.
C001.text:
ArmaturaSec d.o.o. (C001): Cybersecurity, Zrenjanin, 67 employees, founded 2008.
ArmaturaSec d.o.o. has been building network security hardware in Zrenjanin since 2008. We started by selling simple firewall appliances to regional electricity distributors who needed to segment their control networks from corporate IT. Over fifteen years that focus narrowed: today every product we ship is designed specifically for operational technology environments — the kind of networks that run pumps, switchgear, and assembly lines, not office computers. Our customers are energy utilities, water treatment operators, and discrete manufacturers in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. They are not looking for cloud dashboards or vendor lock-in; they need a device that sits in a metal cabinet at a substation or pump station, runs for years without attention, and tells someone when something is wrong. We have 67 people in Zrenjanin. About half write firmware or do hardware bring-up; the rest handle sales, installation, and support. Our head of engineering, Radovan Čičić, joined from a SCADA integrator in 2011 and has led every product generation since. We do not resell other vendors' software. Everything that runs on our appliances — the protocol parsers, the access control engine, the alerting logic — is written and maintained by our own team.
Products: NetGuard-OT: network access control appliance for industrial Ethernet segments; NetGuard-OT Mini: DIN-rail form factor variant for smaller substations and pump stations; ProtoSense: passive protocol inspection module for Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP traffic; ArmaturaSec Managed Support: annual firmware maintenance and remote monitoring subscription; SecAudit Report: one-time on-site assessment and written security findings report.
Tech: Embedded Linux (custom Yocto build); Modbus TCP and BACnet/IP protocol parsing; C and Rust for firmware components; iptables and nftables for packet filtering; GPRS and LTE-M cellular backhaul; Python for internal tooling and test scripts; Hardware-in-the-loop bench testing with physical PLC simulators; X.509 certificate management for device identity.
Plans: ArmaturaSec intends to release a fifth hardware variant in late 2025 with a dedicated security processor to support on-device anomaly detection without affecting packet forwarding latency. We are also evaluating whether to open a small office in Sarajevo to reduce travel time for Bosnian client support.
R&D capacity: We can dedicate one to two engineers part-time to a collaborative project, with access to our traffic archives, our hardware bench, and our existing firmware codebase under NDA.
Past collaborations: We ran a one-semester student project with a technical faculty in Novi Sad in 2021 that produced a prototype BACnet fuzzer; the code was useful but the collaboration was not continued formally.

C001-CH1.title: We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.
C001-CH1.text:
We need to detect unusual behaviour on Modbus and BACnet networks without labelled attack data — our clients have never been breached (or don't know it), so we have zero examples of malicious traffic and supervised classifiers are useless to us.

Our ProtoSense module watches Modbus and BACnet traffic and is supposed to flag anything that looks wrong. The problem is that none of our clients has ever given us a packet capture that contains a confirmed attack. A few of them have been running their networks for twenty years with no security monitoring at all, so if they were compromised they would not know. We have plenty of normal traffic — we have collected several terabytes of captures from consenting clients over the past three years — but we have nothing labelled as malicious. We tried building a supervised classifier once, fed it data from public ICS datasets, and it flagged so many false positives in real deployments that clients started switching the alerts off. What we actually need is something that learns what normal looks like on a specific site and raises a flag when behaviour drifts from that baseline. We have the traffic archives, we have the hardware to run inference on-device, and we have one engineer who has been reading about anomaly detection for six months. We need a method that works with no attack examples and that we can explain to a plant manager in plain language.

C001-CH2.title: Our appliance firmware update process currently requires a technician on-site at the customer's substation; we want secure over-the-air updates, but every approach we've prototyped either has an unacceptable attack surface or fails when the GPRS link drops mid-transfer.
C001-CH2.text:
Our appliance firmware update process currently requires a technician on-site at the customer's substation; we want secure over-the-air updates, but every approach we've prototyped either has an unacceptable attack surface or fails when the GPRS link drops mid-transfer.

Every time we release a firmware update we have to send someone to the customer site to plug in a USB drive. For a substation forty kilometres outside Novi Sad that is manageable. For a client in a mountain valley in Bosnia it means a full day of travel. We want to push updates over the cellular link the appliance already uses for remote monitoring. We have prototyped three approaches. The first used a plain HTTPS pull with a signature check; a security review inside the team found the key storage on the current hardware was not good enough and an attacker with physical access could extract the signing key. The second used a dual-partition scheme with rollback; it worked fine on a stable connection but when the GPRS link dropped mid-transfer the bootloader left the device in a state we could not recover remotely, which is unacceptable at an unmanned site. The third prototype added a download manager with resume support but the code size pushed us over the flash budget on our older hardware variant. We need a design that tolerates interrupted transfers, does not require hardware we cannot retrofit, and does not introduce a new remote code execution path. We have a draft threat model document we can share.

C001-CH3.title: Three clients in Serbia and one in Bosnia asked us to provide a risk quantification report in euros — how much financial loss a specific vulnerability exposes them to — and we have no methodology for that; it's becoming a dealbreaker in contract negotiations.
C001-CH3.text:
Three clients in Serbia and one in Bosnia asked us to provide a risk quantification report in euros — how much financial loss a specific vulnerability exposes them to — and we have no methodology for that; it's becoming a dealbreaker in contract negotiations.

Four clients — three in Serbia and one in Bosnia — have asked us to attach a euro figure to each finding in our SecAudit reports. They want to be able to tell their board: this vulnerability could cost us this much. We understand why they ask. They need to justify remediation budgets. The problem is we have never done this and we are not sure our current data supports it. We have records of what the vulnerabilities were, we know roughly what downtime costs for a water utility or an electricity distributor, and we can find published incident cost studies from Western Europe. What we do not have is a repeatable calculation method that holds up when a procurement officer asks how we arrived at the number. We have looked at two published frameworks and found them either too abstract or built for IT environments where data breach costs dominate. Our clients care about production downtime, regulatory fines under Serbian energy law, and emergency response costs. We need a methodology we can apply consistently across different client types, document in a way that survives scrutiny, and run with our existing audit team without hiring a financial analyst.

C001-CH4.title: Our quality assurance team writes regression tests by hand for every firmware release; with four hardware variants and monthly release cycles that's eating about 35% of total engineering time and we're still shipping bugs that automated tests should catch.
C001-CH4.text:
Our quality assurance team writes regression tests by hand for every firmware release; with four hardware variants and monthly release cycles that's eating about 35% of total engineering time and we're still shipping bugs that automated tests should catch.

We release firmware roughly once a month across four hardware variants: the original NetGuard-OT board, the Mini, and two older boards we still maintain for clients under long-term support contracts. Before each release our QA team runs a regression suite that they have been building by hand since 2015. The suite now has around 1,400 test cases. Writing new cases for a feature, updating old ones when hardware behaviour changes, and running everything on four boards takes about two and a half weeks of engineering time per cycle. That is the 35% figure. We have also shipped three bugs in the past year that the regression suite should have caught but did not because the relevant test cases were out of date. We have tried generating tests from our internal protocol specifications but the tooling we built for that was brittle and the team abandoned it. We want to get to a point where adding a feature automatically produces a skeleton of tests that a junior engineer can complete in an hour rather than a day. We are open to any approach that fits inside our existing Python-based test runner and does not require us to replace the hardware bench we already have.

C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Tryi.id: C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Trying to Use Public ICS Datasets for Anomaly Detection
C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Tryi.title: Why We Stopped Trying to Use Public ICS Datasets for Anomaly Detection
C001/blog/2024-05-20/Why We Stopped Tryi.text: For about eighteen months we tried to build a detection component that could identify unusual Modbus traffic by training on labelled datasets published by research groups. We had four datasets we thought were credible. We spent a significant chunk of time getting them into a format our pipeline could use, training classifiers, and then testing them against real traffic from our own lab bench and from anonymised captures our clients had agreed to share with us. The results were not good. False positive rates that looked acceptable on the test set turned into something much worse when we applied the model to a real site. A water treatment plant runs its Modbus polling on a rhythm that is specific to that plant — the scan rate, the register addresses, the devices on the bus, everything. A model trained on traffic from a research testbed in another country does not know that rhythm. It cannot know it. We also noticed that the labelled datasets we were using represented attack scenarios that were either very obvious (flooding the bus with write commands) or very specific to hardware we do not see in the Balkans. Neither is particularly useful. What we think actually works for our environment is learning what normal looks like on a specific site and flagging deviations from that. No labels, no pre-trained model from somewhere else. This is not a new idea. The challenge is doing it in a way that runs on our hardware, produces alerts that a plant operator can understand without a data science background, and does not require us to collect six months of clean traffic before it is useful. We have not solved this yet. We have a set of traffic archives from our client base and one engineer who has been working on this part-time. If you have relevant experience or want to talk about it, we are interested.

C001/job/2024-02-05/Firmware Engineer —.title: Firmware Engineer — Network Protocols (Zrenjanin)
C001/job/2024-02-05/Firmware Engineer —.text:
ArmaturaSec is looking for a firmware engineer to join our core development team in Zrenjanin. We have a monthly release cycle across four hardware variants and we need someone who can contribute to protocol parsing, system integration, and the tooling that keeps the whole process running. What the work looks like day to day: you will work on the firmware that runs on our NetGuard-OT appliances — mostly C with an increasing share of Rust for new components. You will work closely with the person responsible for our Yocto build system and with the QA team that tests each release on physical hardware. We deal with Modbus TCP, BACnet/IP, and a few less common industrial protocols. You do not need to know all of them when you start. You do need to be comfortable reading protocol specifications and writing parsers from them. The hardware side: our appliances are based on ARM Cortex-A SoCs. We have a bench in the office with physical boards, PLC simulators, and packet generators. You will spend time at that bench. What we are looking for:
— At least three years writing firmware or embedded systems software in C
— Comfort with Linux networking internals (netfilter, raw sockets, that level)
— Experience debugging with JTAG or serial console, not just printf
— Some exposure to Rust is useful but not required What we are not looking for: someone who wants to work on cloud infrastructure or web services. This is hardware-close work. We offer a permanent contract, a salary in line with the Zrenjanin market for this experience level, and flexible hours within reason. The office is in the industrial zone on the north side of the city. Remote work is possible one or two days a week once you are settled in. Send a CV and a short note about something you have built to [email removed].

C001/job/2024-03-12/QA and Test Automati.title: QA and Test Automation Engineer (Zrenjanin)
C001/job/2024-03-12/QA and Test Automati.text:
Our QA team maintains a regression suite of around 1,400 test cases that runs against every firmware release on four hardware boards. The suite is written in Python and runs against physical hardware on a test bench. It works, but it is slow to extend and we are spending too much engineering time on it. We are looking for someone who wants to take ownership of that suite and make it better. That means maintaining what is already there, finding ways to generate or scaffold new test cases faster, and reducing the manual effort involved in keeping tests up to date when firmware behaviour changes. This is not a role where you will be asked to deploy a commercial test management platform and declare victory. We have specific constraints: the test runner is Python, the hardware is physical and will stay physical, and the timeline for releases is not going to change. What we need is someone who will sit with the existing code, understand why it is the way it is, and improve it incrementally. Some things that would be useful background:
— Experience maintaining a large test suite in Python
— Familiarity with hardware-in-the-loop testing or any kind of test automation that involves real devices rather than simulators
— An opinion about why test suites grow brittle over time and what to do about it Experience with industrial protocols is not required. You will learn what you need to know about Modbus and BACnet on the job. The role is full-time in Zrenjanin. One or two days remote per week is possible. We expect some collaboration with our firmware engineers and some with the field support team who often find bugs first. Questions and applications to [email removed]. We review applications on a rolling basis.

C002.title: Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o.
C002.text:
Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o. (C002): Game development, Zrenjanin, 8 employees, founded 2019.
Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o. was founded in 2019 by siblings Miroslav and Tatjana Kovačević, who grew up in Zrenjanin and wanted to build something useful for the region's schools rather than chase the international mobile market. We make browser-based educational games for primary school children in Serbia and Hungary, sold mainly to municipalities, school boards, and NGOs that work in bilingual Serbian–Hungarian communities in Vojvodina. Our games run in any modern browser without installation, which matters in schools where IT budgets are tight and devices are old. Subjects covered include mathematics, Serbian language, Hungarian language, and basic natural sciences for ages six to twelve. We are a team of eight: two developers, one graphic designer, one illustrator, one sound designer, one pedagogy consultant, and two people handling sales, contracts, and support. Tatjana leads product and pedagogy; Miroslav leads development. Most of us have known each other since secondary school or university in Novi Sad. Our customers include the City of Zrenjanin education office, three NGOs operating across Vojvodina, and two municipal education departments in southern Hungary. We work on fixed-price B2B contracts, usually tied to a school year, and we spend real time talking to teachers before we build anything.
Products: Browser-based math games for grades one through four; Serbian and Hungarian language literacy games for early primary; Basic natural-science quiz modules for grades three and four; Custom educational game development for municipalities and NGOs; Annual content-update and hosting service contracts for existing deployments.
Tech: HTML5 / JavaScript (vanilla and Phaser 3 game framework); PHP backend with MySQL for session and score storage; Custom clickstream event logging (JSON over REST); Figma for UI and asset design; Aseprite for pixel-art and sprite animation; Audacity for sound editing; Shared Linux VPS hosting (self-managed); Git with self-hosted Gitea.
Plans: We want to expand our catalogue to cover grades five and six by the end of 2026, and we are exploring a pilot with one Hungarian school district for a fully bilingual game set tied to their local curriculum. We are also considering moving from VPS hosting to a managed cloud setup to reduce maintenance load on Miroslav.
R&D capacity: Miroslav Kovačević is available for roughly one day per week for research-related work, with Tatjana available for pedagogy input on a similar basis, but both are constrained by ongoing contract delivery.
Past collaborations: We worked informally with a primary school teacher network in Zrenjanin — coordinated by a local NGO called Vojvodina Creative Schools — to gather playtesting feedback during the development of our first math module in 2020, but we have no formal research or university collaboration history.

C002-CH1.title: Teachers tell us our math games are fun but they can't see whether a child is actually learning — we have clickstream data for 4,200 students but no way to tell if a pupil is guessing randomly versus genuinely understanding the material.
C002-CH1.text:
Teachers tell us our math games are fun but they can't see whether a child is actually learning — we have clickstream data for 4,200 students but no way to tell if a pupil is guessing randomly versus genuinely understanding the material.

Every time a child clicks an answer in our math games, we log it — timestamp, question ID, answer chosen, how long they took, how many attempts. We have that data for about 4,200 students across the 2022–23 and 2023–24 school years. The problem is we have no way to read anything meaningful out of it. A teacher told us last spring that one of her students had a 91% score but she was convinced the child understood nothing and was just clicking fast until something turned green. She was right — when she tested the child on paper the results were very different. We know this is a real problem but we do not know how to separate genuine learning from lucky guessing using the data we already have. We have exported the logs to CSV and tried building simple accuracy thresholds ourselves, but that does not catch the fast random clicker. We cannot afford to buy an off-the-shelf analytics platform, and we would not trust one that does not explain what it is doing. A good outcome for us would be a method or a small working tool that flags students who are likely guessing, so teachers can act on it. We would ideally have something testable before the 2025–26 school year starts.

C002-CH2.title: We want to make our games accessible to children with dyslexia — about 12% of our user base based on teacher reports — but we don't know which font choices, colour contrasts, and text-presentation speeds actually help versus what is just marketing.
C002-CH2.text:
We want to make our games accessible to children with dyslexia — about 12% of our user base based on teacher reports — but we don't know which font choices, colour contrasts, and text-presentation speeds actually help versus what is just marketing.

About twelve percent of our users have been flagged by their teachers as having dyslexia or suspected reading difficulties. That is based on informal teacher reports, not formal diagnosis, so the real number could be different. Right now we use one standard font across all our games — a rounded sans-serif we picked because it looked friendly — and we set line spacing and reading speeds based on what felt reasonable to us. We have read about OpenDyslexic and similar fonts, and we have seen marketing material from several dyslexia-support tool companies claiming specific font and colour combinations help, but we cannot find solid evidence behind most of those claims that was actually tested with children in a classroom setting rather than adults in a lab. We tried switching one game to a higher-contrast colour scheme after a parent complained and got no useful feedback either way. We do not have the expertise to design a proper test ourselves, and we do not want to run experiments on children without knowing what we are doing. A good outcome would be a clear, evidence-backed set of recommendations for font, contrast, and text presentation speed that we can apply across our whole catalogue in one update cycle.

C002-CH3.title: We applied for an Innovation Fund Voucher six months ago and the application was returned twice for administrative corrections — we don't have the internal capacity to manage grant paperwork and it's pulling our lead developer away from product work for weeks at a time.
C002-CH3.text:
We applied for an Innovation Fund Voucher six months ago and the application was returned twice for administrative corrections — we don't have the internal capacity to manage grant paperwork and it's pulling our lead developer away from product work for weeks at a time.

We applied for an Innovation Fund Voucher for Small Enterprises in early 2024. The application came back twice — once because the project description was categorised under the wrong activity code, and once because a supporting financial document was formatted incorrectly. Both corrections were straightforward once we understood what was needed, but figuring that out took weeks of back-and-forth with the fund administrator, and it was Miroslav who handled it because no one else on the team could. That pulled him away from a game update we had promised to a municipal customer. We are a small company and none of us trained for grant administration. We do not have budget to hire a consultant for every application, and we are likely to apply for other public funding in 2025. What we actually need is either someone who can help us build a reusable internal process for these applications, or a partnership arrangement where a research or support institution co-applies with us and carries the administrative side, while we contribute the product development work.

C002/blog/2024-09-10/What We Learned at.id: C002/blog/2024-09-10/What We Learned at the Novi Sad Education Technology Gathering
C002/blog/2024-09-10/What We Learned at.title: What We Learned at the Novi Sad Education Technology Gathering
C002/blog/2024-09-10/What We Learned at.text: In late August we attended the Novi Sad Education Technology Gathering, a small two-day event for people working on digital tools in Serbian and regional schools. It was the second year it ran and this time drew around ninety attendees — mostly teachers, a few NGO coordinators, a handful of small companies like us, and some people from municipal education offices. We went mainly to listen. We had a small table where people could sit and try our games, and we talked to probably thirty or forty people over the two days. A few things stood out. First, the question of what students actually learn came up in almost every conversation. Teachers are used to seeing scores and completion rates, but several of them said directly that high scores do not always mean real understanding. One teacher from a school in Novi Sad described the same pattern we have been hearing from our own users — children who finish every level quickly but cannot do the same tasks on paper. We are working on this problem and it was useful to hear that it is not specific to our games. Second, there was more interest in accessibility than we expected. Three teachers mentioned dyslexia or reading difficulties without us raising the topic. One asked specifically what we were doing about it. The honest answer is that we are still figuring it out, and we said so. Third, we had a useful conversation with a representative from an NGO called Ravnica Learning Network, which works with schools in rural parts of Vojvodina. They are currently operating under a contract with a different provider but mentioned they would be open to talking in early 2025 when that contract ends. Overall a worthwhile two days. We came back with a clearer picture of what teachers want and a list of conversations to follow up on.

C002/job/2024-06-01/Freelance Data Analy.id: C002/job/2024-06-01/Freelance Data Analyst — Learning Outcomes Project (Short-Term Contract)
C002/job/2024-06-01/Freelance Data Analy.title: Freelance Data Analyst — Learning Outcomes Project (Short-Term Contract)
C002/job/2024-06-01/Freelance Data Analy.text:
We are looking for a freelance data analyst for a defined short-term project, expected to run three to five months. Background: We log clickstream events for every student session across our math games — question ID, answer, timestamp, attempt count, time-on-question. We have roughly 4,200 students' worth of data from the last two school years in CSV exports from our MySQL database. We want to build a simple, explainable method for identifying students who are likely guessing randomly rather than demonstrating understanding. The output needs to be something a classroom teacher can act on without needing to understand statistics. What we are looking for:
- Experience working with behavioural or interaction log data
- Ability to work in Python or R — whichever you prefer
- Interest in making outputs readable for non-technical users (teachers, school coordinators)
- Clear communication — we need to understand what you are doing and why at each step What this is not: This is not a machine-learning research project. We do not need a published paper. We need something that works reliably on the data we have and can be maintained by a small team. Interpretability matters more than accuracy metrics. Data access: We will provide anonymised CSV exports. No personally identifiable information will be included — students are identified only by anonymised session IDs. Budget: Modest. We are a small company. Please ask about the range before applying if that is a concern — we would rather have an honest conversation early. If this sounds like work you would find interesting, write to us at [email removed] with a short description of relevant experience.

C002/news/2024-04-22/New Contract: Subot.id: C002/news/2024-04-22/New Contract: Subotica District Education Office Joins for 2024–25 School Year
C002/news/2024-04-22/New Contract: Subot.title: New Contract: Subotica District Education Office Joins for 2024–25 School Year
C002/news/2024-04-22/New Contract: Subot.text: We are pleased to confirm that the Subotica District Education Office has signed a one-year contract with Zrenjanin Game Works for use of our math and language game modules across fourteen primary schools in the district. This is our first contract in the Subotica area and our largest to date in terms of number of schools. The district serves a significant Hungarian-speaking population, which is part of why they approached us — our Hungarian-language content and the bilingual structure of our games matched what they were looking for. The contract covers our full mathematics module for grades one through four and both the Serbian and Hungarian literacy games. Schools will be onboarded in September at the start of the new school year. We will run two short orientation sessions for teachers in August — one in Subotica and one online — to walk through how the platform works and how to read the session reports. For us, this is a meaningful step. Most of our previous contracts have been in and around Zrenjanin, where we have existing relationships with schools and the education office. Expanding to Subotica means working with teachers we have not met before, in a district with a different demographic mix. We expect to learn a lot. Tatjana Kovačević, who handles pedagogy and customer relationships, will be the primary contact for the Subotica schools throughout the year. If you are a municipality or school district interested in similar arrangements, our contact address is [email removed].

C002/news/2024-10-30/Innovation Fund Vou.id: C002/news/2024-10-30/Innovation Fund Voucher Application: Where We Are
C002/news/2024-10-30/Innovation Fund Vou.title: Innovation Fund Voucher Application: Where We Are
C002/news/2024-10-30/Innovation Fund Vou.text: We want to be straightforward about something that has taken up more of our time than we expected this year. In March 2024 we submitted an application for an Innovation Fund Voucher for Small Enterprises. The application was intended to fund a research collaboration focused on our student learning analytics work. The application was returned in May for corrections related to activity classification, resubmitted in June, returned again in July for a formatting issue in a financial attachment, and resubmitted in August. As of the end of October we are still waiting on a decision. This process has cost us roughly six weeks of Miroslav's working time spread across the year — time that came directly out of product development. We delivered our Subotica contract obligations on schedule, but a planned update to the natural science modules was pushed back by two months as a result. We are not writing this to complain about the fund or the process. The corrections requested were legitimate; we made mistakes in the original application. The problem is that we do not have someone on the team whose job is grant administration, and trying to build that capacity while also running a small software company is genuinely difficult. If the application is approved, the funding would support the analytics work we have described elsewhere. If it is not approved, we will need to find another way to approach that problem, possibly through a partnership arrangement with a research institution that has more experience with public funding applications. We are telling this story publicly because we suspect other small companies in the region are in the same position, and because honesty about how these things actually go seems more useful than pretending the process is smooth.

C002/website/2024-02-10/What We Do — Zre.id: C002/website/2024-02-10/What We Do — Zrenjanin Game Works
C002/website/2024-02-10/What We Do — Zre.title: What We Do — Zrenjanin Game Works
C002/website/2024-02-10/What We Do — Zre.text: We make educational browser games for primary schools. That is the whole job. Our games run directly in a browser — Chrome, Firefox, Edge, it does not matter — on any device the school already has. There is nothing to install, no account for parents to create, and no advertisements. A teacher adds the game link to the classroom portal and children can start playing in the same lesson. We currently cover mathematics for grades one through four, Serbian and Hungarian language literacy for early primary, and a set of natural-science quiz modules for grades three and four. All content is aligned with the Serbian national curriculum, and our language games are available in both Serbian and Hungarian to serve the bilingual communities of Vojvodina. Our customers are municipalities, school boards, and NGOs. We do not sell directly to individual schools or parents. A typical contract covers a one or two-year licence for a defined set of schools, with a content-update and hosting service included. Prices are fixed at contract signing, so there are no surprises mid-year. Before we build anything new, we talk to teachers. Our pedagogy consultant Tatjana Kovačević coordinates playtesting and curriculum-mapping sessions with classroom teachers, usually in Zrenjanin and the surrounding municipalities. We have been doing this since our first game in 2020 and it shapes everything from the difficulty curve to the visual design. If you represent a municipality, school district, or NGO and want to discuss a contract, contact us at [email removed]. We are a small team and we respond personally.

C003.title: AutomVoj a.d.
C003.text:
AutomVoj a.d. (C003): Robotics and industrial automation, Zrenjanin, 212 employees, founded 1983.
AutomVoj a.d. has been building conveyor and sorting automation systems from its base in Zrenjanin since 1983. What started as a small workshop supplying domestic food processing plants has grown into a team of 212 engineers, electricians, and technicians shipping systems to customers in Serbia, Hungary, Romania, Austria, Slovenia, Croatia, and Slovakia. Our core business is straightforward: we design, manufacture, and commission PLC-based conveyor lines and automated sorting equipment for food and beverage producers who need reliable throughput in demanding environments — cold stores, wet wash areas, high-dust packaging halls. We do not chase every sector; we know food and beverage and we do it well. Our fabrication shop, electrical assembly area, and in-house testing floor are all under one roof on our Zrenjanin site. Most of our project managers started as commissioning engineers, so they understand what a line stoppage costs a customer at three in the morning. We have long-term supply relationships with component makers in Germany and Italy and we carry enough spares stock to respond within 48 hours on any system we have installed. Roughly 60 percent of our revenue now comes from repeat customers or referrals.
Products: PLC-controlled conveyor systems for chilled and ambient food production lines; Automated sorting and grading equipment for fruit, vegetable, and packaged goods; Electrical control panels and drive cabinets for industrial automation; On-site commissioning, maintenance contracts, and spare-parts supply; System retrofits and capacity upgrades on legacy conveyor installations.
Tech: Siemens S7-1500 and S7-300 PLC platforms; Ladder logic and structured text programming in TIA Portal; Siemens SINAMICS and SEW-EURODRIVE servo and frequency drive systems; Mild steel and stainless steel MIG/MAG welded frame fabrication; EPLAN Electric P8 for electrical schematic design; Profibus and Profinet industrial networking; HMI development with Siemens WinCC and Weintek panels; AutoCAD Mechanical for conveyor layout and structural drawings.
Plans: AutomVoj intends to increase its export share to 55 percent of revenue within three years, targeting food logistics customers in Central Europe, and is evaluating an entry into automated poultry processing lines as a second vertical. The second assembly hall, once financed, is expected to be operational by mid-2026.
R&D capacity: We have no dedicated R&D department; technical development happens informally through project work, led by our chief engineer and two senior automation engineers who allocate time between live projects and improvement work.
Past collaborations: AutomVoj completed a one-year joint development project with Fakultet tehničkih nauka in Novi Sad in 2019 on drive energy monitoring, which resulted in an internal measurement tool but was not published or commercialised.

C003-CH1.title: Our conveyor frames crack at the weld joints after roughly 18 months of operation in chilled environments; we've replaced 14 assemblies under warranty this year and we can't reproduce the failure in our workshop because we test at room temperature.
C003-CH1.text:
Our conveyor frames crack at the weld joints after roughly 18 months of operation in chilled environments; we've replaced 14 assemblies under warranty this year and we can't reproduce the failure in our workshop because we test at room temperature.

Our conveyor frames are welded from mild steel hollow section and painted for corrosion resistance before delivery. When these systems run in customer cold stores — typically operating between 2 °C and 6 °C — we are seeing weld joint cracking at the main crossmember-to-stringer connections after about 18 months of continuous use. This year alone we have replaced 14 complete frame assemblies under warranty, which is costing us in material, travel, and lost engineer time. The frustrating part is that we have tried to reproduce the failure in our workshop and cannot do it. We test frames under load at room temperature and they pass without any problem. Our suspicion is that the combination of thermal cycling, condensation, and the vibration load from loaded belts is doing something we are not seeing at ambient conditions. We have photos and measurements of the cracked joints from site visits, and we still have two of the failed sections in storage. We do not currently have the equipment or know-how to test at low temperatures under cyclic load. A good outcome would be understanding exactly what is causing the cracks so we can change our welding procedure, filler material, or joint design and stop the warranty replacements.

C003-CH2.title: Our PLC programs for different customers are each a custom spaghetti of ladder logic; when we want to push a safety patch we have to touch 38 separate codebases and it takes three engineers two full weeks.
C003-CH2.text:
Our PLC programs for different customers are each a custom spaghetti of ladder logic; when we want to push a safety patch we have to touch 38 separate codebases and it takes three engineers two full weeks.

Over the years we have written a separate PLC program for almost every customer installation. Each one started from a rough template and then grew as the customer asked for changes during commissioning and after. Today we have 38 active codebases across our installed base, all written in ladder logic in TIA Portal, and they have drifted apart to the point where a safety-related patch — for example, an emergency stop sequence change required by a new machinery directive interpretation — has to be found, adapted, and tested in every single one of them. The last time we did this it took three of our engineers two full weeks, and they still found two sites where the logic was different enough that the standard fix did not apply cleanly. We know the answer is some form of modular library or structured code reuse, but every time we try to start, the daily project load pulls the engineers away. We have one senior PLC programmer, Dragan Ilić, who understands the full picture, but he is also our lead on active commissioning projects. We need a practical approach that does not require us to rewrite everything at once and that our team can actually maintain going forward.

C003-CH3.title: We need a €2 million investment to open a second assembly hall, and our bank wants a three-year cash-flow model with sensitivity analysis that our CFO doesn't have the capacity to prepare before the Q3 deadline.
C003-CH3.text:
We need a €2 million investment to open a second assembly hall, and our bank wants a three-year cash-flow model with sensitivity analysis that our CFO doesn't have the capacity to prepare before the Q3 deadline.

We have planning permission and a cleared site adjacent to our existing building for a second assembly hall, which would let us run two large projects in parallel and cut our delivery lead times significantly. The total investment is around €2 million covering the building shell, electrical infrastructure, and a new overhead crane. We have a bank that is willing to discuss the loan but their condition before they will issue a term sheet is a three-year cash-flow model with sensitivity analysis showing how the business performs under different revenue and cost scenarios. Our CFO, Milena Varga, manages day-to-day financial operations well, but building a robust forward-looking model of this kind is outside what she normally does, and she does not have the time to learn it from scratch before the bank's Q3 deadline, which falls at the end of September 2024. We have the historical financial data — five years of audited accounts, project margin records, and a pipeline of signed and probable orders. We need someone who can structure that data into a credible model and help Milena understand it well enough to present it and answer questions from the bank.

C003-CH4.title: Noise from our servo drives is injecting harmonics back into client factory grids and we've had two complaints from clients whose measurement instruments were affected; we don't have the tools to characterise the emission spectrum properly.
C003-CH4.text:
Noise from our servo drives is injecting harmonics back into client factory grids and we've had two complaints from clients whose measurement instruments were affected; we don't have the tools to characterise the emission spectrum properly.

Two of our clients — a dairy processing plant and a packaged-goods warehouse — have complained in the past year that precision measurement instruments on their production floors are behaving erratically. Both sites use our conveyor systems with Siemens SINAMICS frequency drives on the main drive motors. Our internal investigation points to harmonic current emissions from the drives feeding back into the building's low-voltage grid and causing interference. We have added standard line reactors on both installations as a first step and the complaints have reduced but not stopped. The problem is that we do not have the test equipment to measure the actual emission spectrum on site — we cannot tell our clients what frequencies are being injected, at what levels, or how those compare to the applicable EN standards for harmonic disturbance. Without that data we are guessing at solutions. We would like to characterise the emission properly, understand which part of our drive configuration is most responsible, and arrive at a consistent design rule we can apply to new installations so this does not keep coming up. Budget for this is limited; we are looking for a practical engineering solution, not a research project.

C003/news/2024-04-03/AutomVoj Delivers S.id: C003/news/2024-04-03/AutomVoj Delivers Sorting Line to Kovačević Frozen Foods in Hungary
C003/news/2024-04-03/AutomVoj Delivers S.title: AutomVoj Delivers Sorting Line to Kovačević Frozen Foods in Hungary
C003/news/2024-04-03/AutomVoj Delivers S.text: AutomVoj a.d. has completed the commissioning of a new automated sorting and conveyor system at the Debrecen facility of Kovačević Frozen Foods Kft., a Hungarian producer of frozen vegetable products. The project covered approximately 120 metres of PLC-controlled conveyor, three sorting stations with weight-based divert gates, and a new central control panel integrating the line into the customer's existing building management infrastructure. The system operates in a cold processing environment at approximately 4 °C and was designed and tested to run in those conditions continuously across two production shifts. Project manager Slobodan Marković led the AutomVoj site team for the eight-week commissioning period. Handover took place in late March after a 72-hour acceptance run at full production throughput with no unplanned stoppages. "The Kovačević project was technically straightforward in some ways and more demanding in others," said Marković. "The cold environment puts different demands on the mechanical side, and we were running electrical installation and PLC commissioning in parallel to meet the customer's production restart date. The team managed it." Kovačević Frozen Foods is the third Hungarian customer AutomVoj has supplied in the past four years. The company currently has active installations in six EU member states in addition to its domestic market. For information about project references or delivery timelines, contact AutomVoj sales at [email removed].

C004.title: OsiguroMi d.o.o.
C004.text:
OsiguroMi d.o.o. (C004): Insurtech — embedded micro-insurance and parametric products, Novi Sad, 58 employees, founded 2019.
OsiguroMi d.o.o. je insurtech kompanija iz Novog Sada, osnovana 2019. godine sa jednom idejom: da osiguranje prestane da bude papirologija i postane tihi servis ugrađen u alate koje ljudi već koriste. Umesto da korisnik kupuje polisu na posebnom sajtu, naša tehnologija se integriše direktno u aplikacije za rezervaciju putovanja, agro-platforme i prodajne sisteme organizatora festivala — i polisa nastaje u trenutku transakcije. Radimo sa B2B partnerima širom Srbije i EU: putničkim platformama, zadrugama, organizatorima open-air događaja. Naš tim od 58 zaposlenih dolazi iz osiguranja, softverskog inženjerstva i analize podataka. Osnivači Milena Čabarkapa i Dragan Horvat prethodno su radili u reosiguranju i fintech sektoru, što je oblikovalo naš pristup: prvo model, pa produkt. Ono što nas razlikuje nije marketing — razlikuje nas API koji se može uključiti za manje od jednog radnog dana i parametarski okidači koji ne zahtevaju korisnikov zahtev za naknadu. Isplata se dešava automatski ili ne, na osnovu merljivih podataka: kašnjenje leta, količina padavina, otkazivanje događaja. Nema formulara, nema čekanja. Klijenti naših partnera to retko primete dok im ne zatreba, a onda primete odmah.
Products: Parametarsko osiguranje useva po vremenskim okidačima; Automatsko osiguranje od kašnjenja leta ugrađeno u platforme za rezervaciju; Osiguranje od otkazivanja festivala i open-air događaja; White-label API za ugradnju mikro-osiguranja u aplikacije trećih strana; Nadzorna tabla za B2B partnere sa isplatnom analitikom u realnom vremenu.
Tech: REST API sa OAuth 2.0 autentifikacijom za partnerske integracije; Automatizovana obrada zahteva za naknadu bazirana na pravilima (rules engine); Integracija sa eksternim API-jem za status letova (FlightBridge Data Services); Mreža meteoroloških stanica i RHMZS podaci za agro-proizvode; PostgreSQL baze podataka sa vremenskim serijama za istorijske gubitke; Python okruženje za aktuarsko modelovanje i kalibraciju okidača; Kubernetes orkestracija za skaliranje tokom vršnog prometa rezervacija.
Plans: Do kraja 2025. planiramo da proširimo agro-liniju na Bugarsku i Rumuniju kroz partnerstvo sa regionalnim zadrugama, i da uvedemo novi okidač za osiguranje od mraza. Razmatramo i mogućnost sopstvene licencirane distribucije u još jednoj EU jurisdikciji kako bismo smanjili zavisnost od spoljnih posrednika.
R&D capacity: Imamo jednog internog istraživača za modelovanje podataka i dva seniorna inženjera koji mogu da izdvoje deo kapaciteta za zajedničke projekte, uz uslov da rezultati budu primenjivi u roku od šest do devet meseci.
Past collaborations: U 2022. godini sarađivali smo sa jednom lokalnom softverskom firmom Logosfera d.o.o. na razvoju prototipa nadzorne table za partnere, ali formalna istraživačka saradnja sa akademskim institucijama do sada nije uspostavljena.

C004-CH1.title: Our weather-triggered crop parametric product pays out when measured rainfall at the nearest official station drops below a threshold, but farmers tell us the station is sometimes 30 km away and their field got rain while the station recorded drought — we're paying out when we shouldn't and refusing when we should.
C004-CH1.text:
Our weather-triggered crop parametric product pays out when measured rainfall at the nearest official station drops below a threshold, but farmers tell us the station is sometimes 30 km away and their field got rain while the station recorded drought — we're paying out when we shouldn't and refusing when we should.

Naš agro-proizvod isplaćuje naknadu kada zvanična meteorološka stanica zabeleži količinu padavina ispod ugovorenog praga u određenom periodu. Problem je što najbliža stanica nekad stoji 30 kilometara od parcele — a na tih 30 km može biti planinski venac, rečna dolina ili urbana zona, sve to menja lokalne padavine drastično. Dobijamo povratne informacije od partnera u Vojvodini i Bačkoj da su im isplate stizale kad polje nije ni presušilo, ili da ih nije bilo kad su urod izgubili. Pokušali smo da korigujemo prag na osnovu istorijskih razlika između stanica i terena, ali to je gruba aproksimacija. Imamo pristup RHMZS podacima i podacima tri privatne agrometeo mreže, ukupno oko 140 tačaka merenja u regionu. Razmišljali smo o satelitskim indeksima vlažnosti tla, ali nismo sigurni kako pouzdano spojiti te izvore u jedan okidač. Cilj je da do sledeće sezone ispravljamo isplate na osnovu prostorno tačnijih procena padavina po parceli, bez potpune zamene ugovornog praga.

C004-CH2.title: We process around 9,000 travel-delay claims per month fully automatically, but our internal audit found that 3.1% of payouts were triggered by data errors from the flight-status API rather than genuine delays — that's real money leaking out every month.
C004-CH2.text:
We process around 9,000 travel-delay claims per month fully automatically, but our internal audit found that 3.1% of payouts were triggered by data errors from the flight-status API rather than genuine delays — that's real money leaking out every month.

Mesečno obrađujemo oko 9.000 zahteva za naknadu zbog kašnjenja leta, potpuno automatski, bez ljudskog uvida. Interna revizija za treće tromesečje 2023. pokazala je da je 3,1% isplata aktivirano greškama u podacima dobavljača statusa letova — pogrešni vremenski žigovi, dupli unosi, letovi koji su tehnički otkazani ali su prikazani kao zakašnjeli. To nije zanemarljiv procenat kad govorimo o isplatama u eurima. Trenutno radimo sa jednim eksternim API-jem za status letova. Pokušali smo da uvedemo jednostavna pravila za otkrivanje anomalija, ali lažni alarmi blokiraju legitimne isplate. Potreban nam je metod koji može da proceni verodostojnost dolaznih podataka pre nego što okidač aktivira isplatu — po mogućnosti u realnom vremenu, jer ceo smisao proizvoda je da korisnik dobije obaveštenje pre nego što napusti aerodrom. Imamo log svih prethodnih API poziva i isplata, što ukupno daje oko 340.000 unosa. Budžet za ovo nije neograničen — gledamo rešenje koje može da radi unutar naše postojeće infrastrukture, ne novi sistem od nule.

C004-CH3.title: We want to price parametric festival-cancellation policies based on historical weather and event cancellation data, but we have fewer than 200 historical festival events in our database and standard actuarial methods need far more data points to produce stable loss curves.
C004-CH3.text:
We want to price parametric festival-cancellation policies based on historical weather and event cancellation data, but we have fewer than 200 historical festival events in our database and standard actuarial methods need far more data points to produce stable loss curves.

Razvijamo parametarsko osiguranje za organizatore open-air festivala: polisa se aktivira ako prognoza padavina premašuje prag u danima događaja, ili ako vlast zabrani održavanje zbog vremenskih uslova. Da bismo postavili cenu, trebaju nam stabilne krive gubitaka. Naša baza podataka sadrži nešto ispod 200 istorijskih festival-događaja u regionu sa pratećim vremenskim podacima — to je premalo za klasične aktuarske metode, krive su nestabilne i margine koje treba da naplatimo postaju nekonkurentne. Probali smo da dopunimo bazu podacima iz otvorenih izvora i novinskih arhiva, ali kvalitet i doslednost su neujednačeni. Razmišljamo o tome da iskoristimo meteorološke podatke šire — recimo statistiku ekstrema za svaku regiju i sezonu — pa da model gradimo odozdo prema gore umesto čisto iz istorije događaja. Nemamo kapacitet da to sami izvedemo do kraja, jer naš aktuarski tim broji dve osobe. Konkretan cilj: metodologija za cenovnik koja daje razumne intervale pouzdanosti čak i sa malim skupom istorijskih događaja, primenljiva na različite lokacije u regionu.

C004-CH4.title: We need to appoint a licensed insurance intermediary in Austria to distribute through a Vienna-based travel platform, and the FMA licensing process has been stalled for seven months because our legal representative resigned.
C004-CH4.text:
We need to appoint a licensed insurance intermediary in Austria to distribute through a Vienna-based travel platform, and the FMA licensing process has been stalled for seven months because our legal representative resigned.

Potpisali smo ugovor o distribuciji sa bečkom platformom za rezervaciju putovanja ViennaJourney GmbH i trebalo je da krenemo u prodaju u prvom kvartalu 2024. Međutim, postupak dobijanja licence kod austrijskog regulatora FMA je u zastoju sedam meseci. Naš pravni zastupnik koji je vodio predmet podneo je ostavku prošlog leta i dokumentacija je ostala nedovršena. Pronašli smo novog savetnika, ali procedura kreće praktično ispočetka jer FMA traži određene dokumente overene od lica koje je prvobitno podnelo zahtev. Radi se o regulatornom, a ne tehničkom problemu — ali ima direktan uticaj na prihod jer je ViennaJourney GmbH uvrstio naš proizvod u plan za letnju sezonu. Ne tražimo prečice, tražimo nekog ko poznaje FMA proceduru iznutra i ko može da pomogne da složimo dokumentaciju na način koji neće biti vraćen po treći put. Vremenski pritisak postoji: ako ne dobijemo licencu do maja 2024, partner pomera integraciju za celu sezonu.

C004/blog/2024-01-29/Zašto 3% grešaka u.id: C004/blog/2024-01-29/Zašto 3% grešaka u automatskim isplatama nije sitnica — i šta smo saznali iz revizije
C004/blog/2024-01-29/Zašto 3% grešaka u.title: Zašto 3% grešaka u automatskim isplatama nije sitnica — i šta smo saznali iz revizije
C004/blog/2024-01-29/Zašto 3% grešaka u.text: Kada smo u oktobru 2023. završili internu reviziju isplata za treće tromesečje, broj koji je iskočio bio je 3,1%. Toliko naših automatskih isplata za kašnjenje leta nije trebalo da bude aktivirano — ne zbog greške u polisi, ne zbog prevare korisnika, već zbog loših podataka koji su ušli u sistem pre nego što je okidač uopšte proverio bilo šta. Naš mehanizam za obradu zahteva radi brzo jer mora. Korisnik koji kasni na letu treba obaveštenje dok je još na aerodromu. To znači da sistem donosi odluku za manje od 60 sekundi od momenta kada API za status letova javi promenu. Problem je što taj API ponekad javlja promene koje su artefakti sistema, a ne stvarnost — dupli unosi, let koji je preklasifikovan iz 'otkazano' u 'kasni' iz tehničkih razloga operatera, vremenski žigovi koji ne odgovaraju stvarnom stanju kapija. U apsolutnim brojevima, 3,1% od 9.000 mesečnih zahteva znači oko 279 pogrešnih isplata mesečno. Svaka isplata u ovoj kategoriji iznosi između 15 i 60 EUR. To nije katastrofa, ali je sistematski odliv koji se akumulira. Ono što nismo imali je filter koji bi proveravao konzistentnost dolaznih podataka pre okidača. Sada tražimo upravo to: ne sistem koji usporava obradu, već sloj validacije koji može da identifikuje neverovatne kombinacije podataka i da ih pošalje na kratak ručni pregled ili zadrži 90 sekundi dok ne stigne potvrda iz alternativnog izvora. Ako radite na ovakvim problemima ili imate iskustvo sa detekcijom anomalija u API tokovima u realnom vremenu, otvoreni smo za razgovor.

C004/job/2024-03-05/Oglas za posao: Juni.id: C004/job/2024-03-05/Oglas za posao: Junior aktuar / analitičar gubitaka
C004/job/2024-03-05/Oglas za posao: Juni.title: Oglas za posao: Junior aktuar / analitičar gubitaka
C004/job/2024-03-05/Oglas za posao: Juni.text:
Naš aktuarski tim raste. Tražimo osobu koja želi da uči kroz stvaran posao, a ne kroz simulator. Kontekst: trenutno nas je dvoje u aktuarskom timu. Bavimo se kalibracijom okidača, analizom isplata i razvojem modela za nove proizvode. Projekti na kojima ćeš odmah raditi uključuju modelovanje gubitaka za festival-osiguranje sa ograničenim skupom podataka i poboljšanje prostorne preciznosti agro-okidača. Šta tražimo:
— Završen ili pri kraju studija aktuarstva, matematike, statistike ili srodnog smera
— Funkcionalno znanje R ili Python za statističku analizu
— Sposobnost rada sa nepotpunim i heterogenim skupovima podataka
— Nema potrebe za iskustvom u osiguranju — naučićeš ovde Prednost:
— Iskustvo sa Bayesian metodama ili bootstrapping pristupima za male uzorke
— Osnovno razumevanje extreme value theory Nudi se:
— Mesečna plata 1.600–2.000 EUR neto
— Mentorstvo od strane seniornog aktuara
— Mogućnost finansiranja aktuarskih ispita
— Kancelarija u NTP Novi Sad, fleksibilno radno vreme Očekujemo kratko motivaciono pismo (maksimalno pola strane) i CV na [email removed], naslov 'Junior Aktuar 2024'. Ne tražimo savršenu biografiju — tražimo jasno razmišljanje.

C004/news/2023-11-08/OsiguroMi potpisao.id: C004/news/2023-11-08/OsiguroMi potpisao ugovor sa agro-platformom Polje.rs — pokrivenost za 1.200 gazdinstava
C004/news/2023-11-08/OsiguroMi potpisao.title: OsiguroMi potpisao ugovor sa agro-platformom Polje.rs — pokrivenost za 1.200 gazdinstava
C004/news/2023-11-08/OsiguroMi potpisao.text: OsiguroMi d.o.o. i platforma za upravljanje gazdinstvima Polje.rs potpisali su partnerski ugovor kojim se parametarsko osiguranje useva integriše direktno u Polje.rs mobilnu aplikaciju. Prema uslovima saradnje, korisnici platforme Polje.rs mogu aktivirati vremensku polisu za svoju parcelu kroz dva klika u aplikaciji — bez odlaska kod agenta, bez papira. Polisa se vezuje za katastarsku parcelu korisnika i prati padavine na osnovu dostupnih meteoroloških podataka za odgovarajuću mikrozonu. U prvoj fazi, koja je počela 1. novembra 2023, pokrivenost je dostupna za gazdinstva u Vojvodini i Mačvi. Planirano je proširenje na ostatak Srbije u drugoj polovini 2024. Direktor Polje.rs platforme Aleksandar Mišković izjavio je: 'Naši korisnici su godinama tražili rešenje koje funkcioniše bez birokratije. Ovo je konkretno i merljivo.' Prema internim podacima OsiguroMi tima, u prvih 30 dana od lansiranja aktivirano je oko 1.200 polisa. Okidačka sezona za zimsku pšenicu počinje u aprilu 2024. Ova integracija je prva u agro-sektoru za OsiguroMi i označava ulazak kompanije na tržište koje do sada nije pokrila. Naredni korak je kalibracija modela na osnovu povratnih informacija koje stižu od gazdinstava u pilot periodu.

C005.title: Kardiolink a.d.
C005.text:
Kardiolink a.d. (C005): Medtech and digital health, Novi Sad, 112 employees, founded 2004.
Kardiolink a.d. has been designing and manufacturing cardiac monitoring devices in Novi Sad since 2004. We started as a small team of electrical engineers and cardiologists who believed that continuous ECG monitoring should not require a hospital stay. Twenty years later, we employ 112 people across hardware design, firmware, clinical affairs, and software, and our patches are used by cardiology clinics and remote patient monitoring programmes in fourteen EU countries. Our core product is the KL-Patch line: single-use, adhesive ECG patches that patients wear for up to 72 hours while going about their normal lives. Clinicians receive processed reports through our cloud-based KardioPortal platform. We handle everything from electrode chemistry and PCB layout to the signal processing algorithms and the regulatory documentation that lets our devices reach patients legally. What keeps us grounded is that we manufacture in-house at our Novi Sad facility. We control tolerances, can trace every component, and can respond to field feedback without waiting on a contract manufacturer. Our clinical team works directly with cardiologists at partner clinics to make sure what we ship is actually useful at the bedside, not just impressive on a datasheet. We are a mid-size company and intend to stay close to the product.
Products: KL-Patch 72: 72-hour single-use adhesive ECG monitoring patch; KL-Patch 14: 14-day extended-wear cardiac event recorder; KardioPortal: cloud platform for ECG data management and clinical reporting; KL-Reader: clinic-side docking station and data upload terminal; Custom OEM patch manufacturing for third-party remote monitoring programmes.
Tech: ADS1293 and ADS1298 analog front-end ICs for ECG acquisition; nRF52840 SoC for Bluetooth Low Energy communication and firmware; FreeRTOS on ARM Cortex-M4 for embedded firmware; Lossless ECG compression using modified SZ algorithm; AWS S3 and Glacier tiered storage for signal archives; IEC 62304-compliant software lifecycle toolchain (Jira, Confluence, Polarion); Altium Designer for PCB layout and design verification; Python and MATLAB for signal processing algorithm prototyping.
Plans: Kardiolink plans to launch the KL-Patch 14 in the German and Dutch markets following CE MDR certification and to expand KardioPortal with a structured reporting module aimed at high-volume cardiology outpatient departments. Over the following two years we intend to grow the device fleet to 6,000 active patches per month and bring cloud infrastructure costs back in line with 2022 levels.
R&D capacity: We have twelve people working across hardware, firmware, and algorithm development, with a shared lab equipped for electronics prototyping, signal acquisition testing, and device-level EMC pre-compliance testing.
Past collaborations: Between 2019 and 2021 Kardiolink worked with the engineering faculty in Subotica on a student project to evaluate alternative electrode materials, which informed the adhesive layer redesign in the KL-Patch 72 revision three.

C005-CH1.title: Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz.
C005-CH1.text:
Our 72-hour ECG patch consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is on, which means the battery barely lasts the full wear period in patients who move a lot; we need to cut active current draw by at least 35% without reducing sampling rate below 250 Hz.

The KL-Patch 72 runs on a 54 mAh lithium cell. At rest, current draw is manageable, but the moment Bluetooth is advertising or streaming, we see peaks that push daily consumption to 18 mAh. For an average patient that leaves about 18 mAh in reserve across three days, which is fine. The problem is active patients — people who trigger more frequent data syncs because they are moving and the device is flagging events. In a cardiology population that is not a small group. We have already tuned BLE advertising intervals and moved to BLE 5.0 long-range PHY for some use cases, and we switched to a lower-power MCU variant last year. We are now within a few milliamps of what we think we can achieve through firmware changes alone. We need someone who understands the full power budget — radio duty cycling, ADC configuration, memory access patterns — and can find where the remaining headroom is. The constraint is hard: sampling rate cannot drop below 250 Hz or the clinical validity of the signal is affected. We have instrumented reference hardware in our lab with a Keysight N6705C power analyzer and can provide full current profiles to anyone working on this.

C005-CH2.title: We generate roughly 2 TB of raw ECG signal per month from field devices; our current lossless compression gives us only 3:1 ratio and storage costs at our cloud provider have reached €7,400 per month, which is unsustainable at the patient volume we are projecting for next year.
C005-CH2.text:
We generate roughly 2 TB of raw ECG signal per month from field devices; our current lossless compression gives us only 3:1 ratio and storage costs at our cloud provider have reached €7,400 per month, which is unsustainable at the patient volume we are projecting for next year.

Each KL-Patch 72 device generates roughly 900 MB of raw 16-bit ECG samples over its wear period at 250 Hz across three channels. We are deploying around 2,200 devices per month and growing. Our current pipeline applies a lossless compression step before upload, and the best we consistently achieve is 3:1, which still leaves us pushing about 2 TB to cloud storage each month. At €7,400 per month that is already a significant operating cost, and if we hit our projected 4,000 devices per month by Q2 next year the bill more than doubles. We looked at moving to lossy compression but our regulatory submission is built around lossless, so changing that requires a new clinical validation study and amendments to the technical file — not something we can do quickly. We also explored cold storage tiering and that saves maybe 15%, not enough. What we actually need is a better lossless algorithm that understands the structure of ECG signals: the quasi-periodic nature, the baseline wander, the noise characteristics of a wearable electrode. We have a labelled dataset of about 140,000 30-minute segments we can share under NDA for algorithm development and benchmarking.

C005-CH3.title: Our CE MDR technical file was submitted eight months ago and the notified body has come back with 23 queries about our software lifecycle documentation under IEC 62304; we do not have in-house regulatory affairs staff experienced with the new MDR annexes and hiring one is taking longer than expected.
C005-CH3.text:
Our CE MDR technical file was submitted eight months ago and the notified body has come back with 23 queries about our software lifecycle documentation under IEC 62304; we do not have in-house regulatory affairs staff experienced with the new MDR annexes and hiring one is taking longer than expected.

We submitted our CE marking technical file under MDR in July last year. The notified body, Zertivo GmbH, came back four months later with 23 written queries. About 18 of the 23 concern our software lifecycle documentation under IEC 62304, specifically the traceability between our risk management records under ISO 14971 and the software safety classification rationale, and the completeness of our verification and validation activity records. We built our QMS years ago under the old MDD and have been adapting it incrementally, but the MDR annexes — particularly Annex I and the software-specific parts of Annex II — are much more demanding. We have two quality engineers on staff who are competent at our manufacturing QMS but have not worked through an MDR submission before at this level of detail. We posted a regulatory affairs manager role three months ago and have not found the right candidate. We need practical help drafting responses to these 23 queries and updating the underlying documentation. The notified body has given us a six-month window to respond before the file lapses. Missing that window means restarting the submission, which would cost us at minimum one full year and delay entry into two new national markets.

C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware En.id: C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware Engineer — Low-Power BLE Systems
C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware En.title: Embedded Firmware Engineer — Low-Power BLE Systems
C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware En.text:
Kardiolink is looking for an embedded firmware engineer to join our device team in Novi Sad. The role sits within a group of five firmware engineers responsible for the software running on our KL-Patch devices. What you will work on: Our patches run FreeRTOS on an ARM Cortex-M4, with a Nordic Semiconductor nRF52840 handling both application logic and BLE communication. The work involves writing and optimising firmware for real-time ECG acquisition at 250 Hz, managing BLE duty cycling to reduce active current draw, and maintaining the IEC 62304-compliant software lifecycle artefacts our notified body requires. We have a specific near-term problem we need help with: our 72-hour patch consumes more current during BLE activity than we want, and we need an engineer who can dig into the power budget at the level of radio scheduler configuration, ADC sampling modes, DMA transfers, and sleep state transitions. We have a Keysight N6705C power analyser set up in the lab and a suite of instrumented reference boards ready to go. What we are looking for:
- Three or more years writing firmware in C for Cortex-M microcontrollers
- Direct experience with Nordic nRF52 series and the nRF5 SDK or nRF Connect SDK
- Demonstrated work on BLE power optimisation: advertising intervals, connection parameters, PHY selection
- Familiarity with FreeRTOS task scheduling and its interaction with low-power modes
- Ability to write and maintain IEC 62304 software lifecycle documentation is a significant plus
- Experience with biosignal acquisition hardware is welcome but not required The position is full-time, on-site in Novi Sad, with some flexibility for remote days after an initial settling-in period. Salary is negotiable based on experience. Send your CV and a short note about a power optimisation problem you have solved to [email removed].

C006.title: PravniPilot a.d.
C006.text:
PravniPilot a.d. (C006): Legal tech, Subotica, 78 employees, founded 2012.
PravniPilot a.d. was founded in 2012 in Subotica by a small team of practicing lawyers and software developers who were tired of spending hours manually searching court archives. We started with a simple keyword-search tool for Serbian civil cases and, over twelve years, grew that into a full AI-assisted research and case-prediction platform now used by 230 law firms in Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our platform ingests published court decisions, extracts key legal arguments, and gives lawyers a structured view of how similar disputes have been decided. The prediction module estimates probable outcome ranges for commercial, labor, and property disputes. We do not replace legal judgment — we give lawyers faster access to better evidence so their judgment is better informed. Our development office sits inside NTP Novi Sad, where most of our engineering and data team works. The Subotica headquarters handles commercial, finance and client relations. Across both offices we employ 78 people, roughly half of them with legal backgrounds. Our current customers range from two-partner boutique firms in Banja Luka to mid-size litigation practices in Zagreb and Belgrade. We have processed over two million court decisions and continue to add new documents daily. We are not the fastest-growing company in legal tech, but our retention rate — 91% of firms renew annually — tells us we are building something genuinely useful.
Products: AI-assisted legal research portal with full-text search across three jurisdictions; Case-outcome prediction module for commercial, labor and property disputes; Document annotation and summary tool with source citation; Court-decision bulk data export API for enterprise customers; Custom legal dataset licensing for insurers and financial institutions.
Tech: Python (data pipelines and ML model training); PyTorch for transformer-based text classification; Elasticsearch for full-text document indexing; PostgreSQL for structured case metadata; React front-end with TypeScript; Docker and Kubernetes on-premises cluster at NTP Novi Sad; Custom PDF and HTML parser for court-document ingestion; Internal annotation tool for labeling case outcomes.
Plans: PravniPilot intends to launch a German-language pilot of its research platform with at least five German law firms by mid-2026, contingent on completing the Series A round. In parallel, the company plans to release a public confidence-scoring API for legal summaries that smaller legal-tech vendors in the region can license.
R&D capacity: Our development team of 14 engineers and two data scientists can allocate roughly two days per week to collaborative research work, provided any research output can be integrated directly into the production codebase.
Past collaborations: PravniPilot ran a six-month data-labeling project with a Novi Sad-based language annotation firm, LinguaNova d.o.o., in 2022 to produce a cleaned subset of Croatian court decisions, but has no current active research partnerships.

C006-CH1.title: Our case-outcome prediction model achieves only 61% accuracy on commercial-dispute rulings from Serbian courts, which is barely better than a lawyer's gut feeling; we suspect the problem is that our training set has only 9,000 labelled decisions and courts don't publish enough structured data.
C006-CH1.text:
Our case-outcome prediction model achieves only 61% accuracy on commercial-dispute rulings from Serbian courts, which is barely better than a lawyer's gut feeling; we suspect the problem is that our training set has only 9,000 labelled decisions and courts don't publish enough structured data.

Our prediction model was trained on roughly 9,000 labeled commercial-dispute decisions from Serbian courts. At 61% accuracy it is not meaningfully better than what an experienced lawyer estimates from memory. We have tried basic data augmentation and have experimented with pre-trained multilingual models fine-tuned on our corpus, but neither moved the needle past 63% in internal tests. The core problem is data volume: Serbian courts do not publish decisions in a consistent machine-readable format, so each document requires significant cleaning before it can be labeled. We have one full-time data engineer and two part-time annotators working on this. We estimate we need at least 40,000 clean, labeled decisions to reach accuracy worth advertising. We are open to exploring transfer learning from Croatian or Bosnian court data, semi-supervised labeling, or better feature extraction from judgment text. A good outcome would be reaching 75% accuracy on a held-out test set within 12 months, which would let us market the prediction feature with honest confidence intervals rather than quietly downplaying it.

C006-CH2.title: We are trying to raise a €2.5 million Series A round to fund expansion into the German legal market but all three venture funds we spoke to in Q1 said our cap table structure is too messy from the 2019 convertible note round; we need legal restructuring advice, not technology.
C006-CH2.text:
We are trying to raise a €2.5 million Series A round to fund expansion into the German legal market but all three venture funds we spoke to in Q1 said our cap table structure is too messy from the 2019 convertible note round; we need legal restructuring advice, not technology.

In 2019 we issued a convertible note to bridge a funding gap. The terms were set in a hurry and the resulting cap table now shows overlapping anti-dilution provisions that make it hard for a new lead investor to model their ownership cleanly. We have spoken with three regional venture funds this year, all of whom expressed interest in the product but pulled back after reviewing our shareholder agreement. Our target is a €2.5 million Series A to fund a German market entry, including translation of the platform and local business development hiring. We need a corporate lawyer with cross-border experience in Serbian and EU startup financing to help us clean up the note terms, renegotiate with the existing noteholders, and produce a cap table that a German or Austrian fund can read without confusion. This is not a technology problem. We have a moderate budget for legal advisory work and a soft deadline of Q3 this year if we want to start German operations before end of 2025.

C006-CH3.title: Law firm users copy our AI-generated research summaries directly into briefs without reading them, and twice this year the summaries contained an outdated precedent; we need a way to attach confidence scores and source provenance to every generated sentence.
C006-CH3.text:
Law firm users copy our AI-generated research summaries directly into briefs without reading them, and twice this year the summaries contained an outdated precedent; we need a way to attach confidence scores and source provenance to every generated sentence.

We generate paragraph-level summaries of relevant court decisions and legal arguments. Several law firm users have told us they paste these summaries directly into draft briefs without checking the source. Twice this year a summary referenced a precedent that had been overturned or amended, and in one case a firm submitted a brief containing the outdated citation before catching the error. We take this seriously. What we want to build is a system that attaches a confidence score and a direct source link to every sentence or claim in a generated summary, so a lawyer can see at a glance whether a statement is based on one decision or fifty, and how recent the most recent supporting case is. We have experimented with simple retrieval-augmented generation, but sentence-level provenance tracking in a multilingual legal context is harder than it looks. We have budget for one additional engineer and are willing to explore collaboration with external research groups. The hard requirement is that the solution works inside our existing React interface without requiring a workflow change for the lawyer.

C006-CH4.title: We store full-text court decisions for three jurisdictions and search response time has degraded from 0.4 seconds to 3.1 seconds since we crossed 2 million documents; our database engineers say we need a fundamentally different indexing architecture.
C006-CH4.text:
We store full-text court decisions for three jurisdictions and search response time has degraded from 0.4 seconds to 3.1 seconds since we crossed 2 million documents; our database engineers say we need a fundamentally different indexing architecture.

When we crossed two million documents in our Elasticsearch cluster last autumn, average search response time climbed from 0.4 seconds to 3.1 seconds. Our two database engineers have tried index sharding, query caching and hardware upgrades, and we got the time down to 2.4 seconds, but that is still unacceptable for a tool lawyers use dozens of times a day during trial preparation. The problem is that our index was designed for a corpus of a few hundred thousand documents and has not been fundamentally rethought since. We are adding roughly 15,000 new documents per month across three jurisdictions, so the situation will keep getting worse. We are open to replacing Elasticsearch with a different architecture, moving to a vector-based semantic search layer, or a hybrid approach, but any solution must support our existing boolean filter queries, multilingual text and our API contract with enterprise customers. Downtime during migration is a serious concern — we cannot afford more than a four-hour maintenance window. Budget for infrastructure changes is available but we would prefer a phased approach.

C006/job/2024-03-18/Database Engineer —.title: Database Engineer — Search Infrastructure
C006/job/2024-03-18/Database Engineer —.text:
